Election officials will recount all of the ballots cast for and against a $73 million tax increase to benefit Jeffco Public Schools after a final tally showed the measure passing by just 327 votes.

“Every vote matters, and when an election comes down to a handful of votes, we want voters to have complete confidence in the outcome,” Jefferson County Clerk and Recorder Amanda Gonzalez said in a statement Friday announcing the recount.

Under state law, a recount is triggered if the margin between passing and failing is one half of one percent or less. Gonzalez said the recount will start Nov. 24 and be completed by Dec. 4.

There’s a lot at stake for Jeffco Public Schools, which is under financial pressure due to declining enrollment. District leaders have said Jeffco, Colorado’s second largest district with 74,000 students, needs the money to stave off further budget cuts.

Most AI tools don’t help students learn. Education-specific AI tools aren’t necessarily better than general purpose chatbots. And even tools that help teachers save time can have unintended consequences for students.

Those are the conclusions from a review of 52 studies on the use of artificial intelligence in educational settings released Tuesday by the AI Hub for Education, part of Stanford University’s SCALE Initiative, which studies which classroom interventions and tools actually work.

The authors of the report aren’t throwing in the towel on AI in education. There is still very little research on AI in K-12 settings in the United States — many of the studies come from other countries or involve college students — and the technology has potential to provide personalized assistance for students and remove some of the tedium from teachers’ jobs.

That potential is worth developing, said Susanna Loeb, faculty director at the SCALE Initiative and an author of the report.

AI tools can be “quite powerful,” Loeb said, to differentiate lessons for students at different levels or support students learning a new language. “You just have to…

items.title: With free-tuition promises, some colleges try to untangle confusion over what they cost
items.summary:
MIDDLEBURY, Vt. — Stately buildings of Vermont limestone surround meticulously tended lawns at the edge of a New England village that looks like it’s the setting for a Hallmark Christmas movie.

There’s a golf course on this campus. The student-faculty ratio is an exclusive 9-to-1. And an undergraduate tour guide is telling visiting prospective applicants about a classmate who spent a semester learning how to forage in Malaysia. 

Middlebury College looks and sounds … expensive. But like other universities and colleges, it’s working hard to persuade people that it’s not.

Middlebury has announced that, starting next year, students from families with annual household incomes up to $175,000 can enroll tuition-free . It becomes the latest of a growing number of schools to make this kind of promise, including Princeton (for most families earning up to $250,000, with typical assets), the University of Chicago ($250,000), MIT ($200,000), Harvard ($200,000), Swarthmore ($200,000) and Davidson ($175,000).

These may seem like generous expansions of financial aid; after all, $175,000 is more than double the nation’s median household income . But while it’s true that few additional families will benefit — 35 to 50 in the incoming class at Middlebury, which typically enrolls about 630 new students per year, the college says — most people in those earnings categories already attend without having to pay tuition.

items.title: Ofsted’s menacing inspections are still disastrous. Schools should answer to the communities they serve | Simon Jenkins
items.summary:
For all the supposed improvements, inspectors still obsess over statistics and adjectives, but surely school success depends on teachers and parents

The government regulation of state schools by Ofsted in England is a fiasco. Following the 2023 suicide of the Reading headteacher Ruth Perry, after her school was downgraded from outstanding to inadequate, Ofsted appears to have referred to a dictionary. Single words were replaced by colour-coded report cards, which use a wider range of different adjectives to grade abstractions such as personal development and wellbeing, achievement and leadership. Never has the concept of “education” seemed so empty.

The reaction of the teaching profession to the new code has itself been devastating, as highlighted in a recent survey that showed more than half of headteachers in England polled after their schools were inspected under Ofsted’s new regime are now considering early retirement as a result of the experience. This sense of misery was also illustrated in a poll conducted by the National Education Union one year on from the introduction of the new framework, with 65% saying it is the same as or worse than before.

Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist

Robert F. Smith STEAM Academy will close at the end of the school year after the Denver school board voted 4-2 Thursday to shutter it. The high school, which was modeled on historically Black colleges and universities, has just 24 students this year.

Board Vice President Monica Hunter and member John Youngquist voted no. Hunter, a former Denver teacher who works for the statewide teachers union, asked about pausing the vote until an agreement granting concessions to teachers at the school could be finalized.

Superintendent Alex Marrero said the school district was done negotiating. He said the two sides verbally agreed on a $1,000 payment to the teachers, plus protections for international teachers with work visas. Marrero said the district rejected other requests. Hunter said those included giving non-tenured teachers two paid days off to interview for other jobs.

“The rationale is this is precedent setting,” Marrero said, “and potentially we have some more (school) consolidations coming, and it would not behoove us to honor those indefinitely.”

items.title: STUDENT VOICE: Schools teach students what to learn, but rarely teach them how to learn
items.summary:
Schools spend years teaching algebra, chemistry and history to students. Yet too many finish high school without knowing how memory, attention and stress impact their learning. They assume that poor grades mean “they aren’t smart enough.”

The truth is, few students are taught evidence-backed strategies for studying, getting a good night’s sleep and managing stress before high-pressure exams.

If schools and teachers want students to thrive, they must teach them how to learn early on.

Case in point: My high school classmate pulled an all-nighter before an Advanced Placement U.S. History exam at Lithonia High School in metropolitan Atlanta, cramming Heimler’s History videos. During the test, he forgot much of the content he had studied. His conclusion was clear: “Maybe I should’ve studied harder.”

I disagreed. The issue wasn’t his effort. Nor his intelligence. It was that he had never been taught how learning worked.

Related: A lot goes on in classrooms from kindergarten to high school. Keep up with our free weekly newsletter on K-12 education .

This is a significant issue for students in under-resourced communities, where access to guidance on how stress, sleep and attention affect learning is often limited .

Many students are left to figure out effective strategies on their own. I saw this firsthand at my school. It’s why I started the Cognition Club in ninth grade with the support of my counselor. As the club developed, we discussed foods that support concentration and strategies for managing stress while studying for the state-required Georgia Milestones Assessment…
items.t: STUDENT VOICE: Schools teach students what to learn, but rarely teach them how to learn

items.title: Sold a story: Get ready!
items.summary:
This podcast, Sold a Story, was produced by APM Reports and reprinted with permission. 

Sold a Story is an investigative podcast about how kids learn — what works in the classroom, the science behind those insights and why that research often doesn’t make it into schools. Season 1 revealed why so many kids are struggling to learn how to read, and it sparked a wave of change across the country. In Season 2, we go beyond reading to look at teaching itself. 

Engelmann’s Direct Instruction has a strong evidence base — so why is it so hard to find in schools? We look at why schools keep giving it up and visit a charter network in North Carolina that’s stuck with it for more than a quarter century.

One of New York City’s more high-profile efforts to tackle the youth mental health crisis after the pandemic appears to be in limbo, and Health Department officials refuse to say whether they plan to renew a service that has drawn scrutiny.

Teenspace launched under former Mayor Eric Adams in November 2023 to provide local teens with free therapists by text, phone, or video chat. The Department of Health and Mental Hygiene signed a three-year contract for $26 million with the platform.

Roughly 52,000 teens had signed up for Teenspace as of last week, Health Department officials told Chalkbeat. About 80% were students of color, they added. Teletherapy services such as Teenspace are hailed as an innovative way to help teens confront stress, anxiety, and depression in a way that feels comfortable for them: by texting. For some New York City teens, the platform was their first encounter with a therapist.

Most of the efforts for public schools to get in on a new federal tax credit have been macro: Public education boosters are creating organizations to grant scholarships for tutoring or SAT prep across an entire school district, state, or region of the country.

But a new effort in Denver is micro. Here, parents are launching an organization to grant scholarships at just three public schools: East High, Morey Middle, and McAuliffe International.

“The general concept is as a parent, if I’m going to give a donation, I’d like to see it impact my neighborhood school,” said East High parent Greg Graeber.

This type of experimentation and parental choice is allowed under the federal tax credit program, a major school choice expansion that’s projected to raise billions of dollars for private school tuition and other educational expenses. The program works like this: Taxpayers will receive a federal tax credit of up to $1,700 if they donate to a scholarship-granting organization. Those organizations then give money to qualifying students.

items.title: TEACHER VOICE: The future of personalized learning cannot be built on technology alone
items.summary:
By the time many of my high schoolers enter my algebra classroom, they already know what their school thinks they are bad at. They carry labels before they ever open a notebook: “remedial,” “unmotivated,” “low-performing.”

Too often, personalized learning begins with those labels. We start with a low score or what we believe students cannot do — a missing skill or an academic gap — and then build instruction around fixing it.

I think we should start somewhere else: with what students care about, what they want to become and what already makes sense to them.

The starting point matters because personalized learning is supposed to do more than respond to academic gaps. Personalized learning is supposed to tailor instruction and learning experiences to support a student’s individual strengths, needs, interests, goals and pace.

But whether it fulfills that promise depends on the information we choose to prioritize . That prioritization matters even more as artificial intelligence becomes a bigger part of personalized learning.

Related: A lot goes on in classrooms from kindergarten to high school. Keep up with our free weekly newsletter on K-12 education . 

AI gives teachers like me new ways to adapt instruction quickly. It can create practice problems, adjust reading levels, provide immediate feedback and generate materials based on student needs. But technology can only personalize the information we choose to give it.

That is why I believe a better approach to personalized learning with AI is giving it information to build learning from the student’s interests and…
items.t: TEACHER VOICE: The future of personalized learning cannot be built on technology alone

items.title: OPINION: That Thanksgiving construction-paper hand turkey on your fridge is actually an education policy failure
items.summary:
You may remember a teacher handing you construction paper every November and telling you to trace your hand and turn each finger into a colorful feather. Maybe you had permission to pick the colors for each feather. Maybe you glued on a single wobbly eye. 

But the product, the process and the definition of success for that project had already been decided. You made a hand turkey. 

Here’s why I hate hand turkeys. 

I suspect that no one asked what you wanted to create. The point was to follow the steps, fill the wall with 25 near-identical Stepford birds and call it art. 

I am 100 percent sure that no one explained how or why a construction-paper turkey became the elementary-school-age equivalent of a meditation on Thanksgiving gratitude. 

This wasn’t an accident of a holiday tradition run amok or even poor practice on anyone’s part. It reflects the residue of dated arts education policies. 

Related: A lot goes on in classrooms from kindergarten to high school. Keep up with our free weekly newsletter on K-12 education . 

Visual art and music have been a formal part of the American public education system since the 19th century. However, for most of that history, they were treated as “specials” or were relegated to “extracurricular engagement.” That began to shift in 1994, when arts educators authored the first national arts standards and federal law named the arts a core academic subject. 

Still, the standards were voluntary, and the accountability systems that reshaped math and reading never extended to the arts. Most states went on to adopt their own arts learning…
items.t: OPINION: That Thanksgiving construction-paper hand turkey on your fridge is actually an education policy failure

items.title: Takeaways from our report on school closures in the US
items.summary:
The start of a new school year can be nerve-racking under any circumstances. But for thousands of students across the U.S., this academic year brought the added difficulty of adjusting to an entirely new school after their previous ones shuttered.

As U.S. birth rates continue a multi-decade slide and state and federal education funding dries up, an increasing number of cash-strapped school districts around the country have resorted to closing campuses to save money. 

At the same time, new research shows student enrollment has fallen much faster than schools are closing, suggesting more painful financial choices lie ahead.

AP is covering school closures in partnership with The Hechinger Report and Big Local News at Stanford University. These are some takeaways from their reporting.

A total of 1,156 U.S. schools closed during the last academic year — the highest number since the pandemic, according to an analysis of federal data by Big Local News at Stanford University. 

For example, the Vallejo City Unified School District, a working-class district near San Francisco, serves half as many students as it did two decades earlier. District leaders have closed five campuses since 2025 — a quarter of its schools. They’ve also placed up to a third of all staff positions on the chopping block to help plug a staggering $36 million deficit.

In Vallejo, a city still struggling to bounce back from the closure of a naval base in the 1990s, school enrollment has tumbled from nearly 18,000 in the fall of 2006 to about 9,300, according to the district. But school districts throughout…
items.t: Takeaways from our report on school closures in the US

items.title: 5 reports, 5 different conclusions about fairness in school funding
items.summary:
“And nationally, schools in predominantly nonwhite districts receive $23 billion less in annual funding than their heavily white counterparts, according to a 2019 analysis by EdBuild.”

— Nikole Hannah-Jones, The New York Times, Oct. 4, 2026

“Contrary to common narratives, high-poverty and predominantly non-white districts have spent about the same as or more per pupil than their more advantaged counterparts for decades.”

— Sarah Reber, Brookings Institution, July 2026 ( Updated Nov. 9, 2026* )

If you’re confused about whether America’s public schools are shortchanging poor children or spending less money educating Black, Hispanic and Native American children, I was too. At least five major reports on school funding released in the past decade have reached conflicting conclusions. Some say disadvantaged students get more money than their wealthier, whiter peers. Others find substantial spending gaps in the opposite direction. 

Why the strikingly different conclusions? Some reports count federal dollars for education, while others exclude them, and some adjust the dollars for regional differences in salaries or other expenses.

The five school spending reports — from Brookings , EdBuild , the Urban Institute , EdTrust and the Education Law Center — all use slightly different methodologies. One dates back to 2017 while another was just released last month.

items.title: OPINION: Higher education has many important stories to tell. So, let’s hear them
items.summary:
Higher education is at least partly responsible for its slide in public trust and perceived value to society. It needs to act now to restore confidence in its usefulness.

The loss of trust is real and across the board. The proportion of Americans who say a college education is “very important” has dropped to an all-time low of 31 percent, according to a 2026 Gallup poll. This was a four-percentage-point drop since 2025 and the lowest share since Gallup first asked the question in 1978. As recently as 2013, 70 percent of Americans in a Gallup survey said college was “very important.” 

However, every semester, in a course I teach on reputation management, when I have my students do a SWOT (strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats) analysis on themselves and ask about their most important strength, they invariably answer something along the lines of, “being at a university, learning how to learn and preparing myself for an uncertain future.”

Related: Interested in innovations in higher education? Subscribe to our free biweekly higher education newsletter . 

Americans in general, like my students, still value higher education’s ability to deliver certain outcomes : A Lumina-Gallup survey in 2025 found that a solid majority of Americans believed that higher education drives innovation, helps create businesses and leads to better jobs. 

The research shows that two things can be true at the same time: “I have less trust in your value than I did; you’re still important to me.” 

Many institutions implicitly assumed that their value was obvious. They believed that if…
items.t: OPINION: Higher education has many important stories to tell. So, let’s hear them
